name: Dihydrofolate reductase deficiency
aliases: megaloblastic anaemia due to DHFR deficiency
cerebral folate deficiency due to DHFR deficiency

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme that reduces dihydrofolate, and dietary folic acid, to active tetrahydrofolate
Presents in infancy with megaloblastic anaemia together with cerebral folate deficiency
Neurological features include seizures, developmental delay and, in some, features overlapping cerebral folate deficiency syndromes
Cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate is characteristically low despite normal or high blood folate
The therapeutic key is that reduced folates such as folinic acid bypass the enzymatic block, whereas ordinary folic acid is ineffective because it requires DHFR to be activated
Folinic acid crosses into the central nervous system and is needed to correct the cerebral folate deficit
Diagnosis is supported by the blood picture, cerebrospinal fluid folate and DHFR gene sequencing
It should be distinguished from cerebral folate deficiency due to folate receptor (FOLR1) defects and from nutritional folate deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate from dihydrofolate produced during thymidylate synthesis and also performs the initial reduction of dietary folic acid to usable reduced folates. When the enzyme is deficient, the supply of tetrahydrofolate and its derivatives, including the 5-methyltetrahydrofolate needed in the central nervous system and the folate cofactors required for nucleotide synthesis, falls. Impaired DNA synthesis in the marrow produces megaloblastic anaemia, while depletion of reduced folate in the brain causes cerebral folate deficiency with seizures and developmental problems. Because folic acid needs this same enzyme to become active, treatment relies on already-reduced folates such as folinic acid.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral folate deficiency due to FOLR1 (folate receptor) defects
Vitamin B12 deficiency and cobalamin metabolism defects
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film showing megaloblastic anaemia
Serum and red cell folate and vitamin B12
Brain MRI in the neurological presentation
Bone marrow examination where the anaemia is unexplained
redFlags: Seizures and developmental regression indicating cerebral folate deficiency
Low cerebrospinal fluid folate despite adequate blood folate
Failure to respond to folic acid, signalling the need for reduced folate
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and treatment using reduced folates the haematological abnormality corrects and neurological outcome can be favourable, but delayed treatment of the cerebral folate deficit may leave lasting neurological impairment.
pitfalls: Prescribing folic acid, which cannot be activated when DHFR is deficient, instead of folinic acid
Being reassured by normal or high blood folate while cerebrospinal fluid folate is low
Overlooking the diagnosis in an infant with megaloblastic anaemia and seizures
Confusing it with FOLR1-related cerebral folate deficiency or nutritional deficiency
references: Banka S et al. Dihydrofolate reductase deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia and cerebral folate deficiency
Blau N. Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
